newsitem.title: USA: U.S. high court to decide affirmative action case.
newsitem.headline: U.S. high court to decide affirmative action case.

text.p: The Supreme Court on Friday rejected the Clinton administration's advice in a major affirmative action case and agreed to decide whether racial diversity can be outlawed as a basis for workplace decisions.

The high court said it would review a closely watched ruling that a New Jersey school district may not take racial diversity into account when laying off a white teacher over an equally qualified black teacher.

The Clinton Justice Department this month urged the high court not to hear the case. It took the awkward position of urging the Supreme Court to leave in place the ruling, even though it did not agree with it.

Department lawyers privately said their strategy reflected fears the Supreme Court may use the case to further restrict, if not end altogether, certain affirmative action programmes for blacks and other minorities.
At issue was an appeal by the Board of Education in Piscataway arguing that employers may consider race as a factor in layoff decisions for purposes other than to remedy past discrimination.

The school board argued that fostering diversity on a high school faculty was a lawful purpose and said consideration of race in layoff decisions does not invariably violate the rights of white employees.
The case may have far-reaching implications for affirmative action, which President Bill Clinton has long supported with his policy to "mend it, don't end it."
Clinton said Friday he was exploring "what our legal options are" to preserve preferential admission policies for minority students at federally-funded colleges and universities.
In a question-and answer session with a group of Hispanic-Americans, Clinton said, "I'm not willing to give up on affirmative action in education." He made no mention of the New Jersey case.
The Supreme Court will hear arguments in the case during its 1997-98 term that begins in October, with a decision likely next year.

School board attorney David Rubin said the case "has become the lightning rod in a stormy national debtate" on whether the civil rights law allows schools to consider race in employment decisions "to foster a diverse learning environment."

Under the Republican Bush administration, the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division backed the discrimination lawsuit by Sharon Taxman, the white business teacher at the high school who lost her job in 1989.
In 1994, the Democratic Clinton Justice Department switched sides to support the school board.

The Justice Department took yet another position in its Supreme Court filing, saying the appeal should be denied because of certain peculiarities in the case. But it still said the appeals court was wrong.
The Supreme Court in recent years has moved to restrict government affirmative action programmes, which flourished in the 1960s and 1970s as a way to remedy past discrimination.
The high court in 1995 restricted federal affirmative action programmes for racial minorities, setting tough new standards before the government can pursue preferences for blacks or other minorities.

The school laid off Taxman instead of black teacher Debra Williams, who had been hired on the same day in 1980. Williams was the only black teacher in the business education department. Taxman returned to work in 1991 when another position opened up in the business department.
